utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for today. Starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Daniel Saxon for the Prosecution, with my colleagues April Carter and Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Eric Tully, and Gregor Guy-Smith appearing on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And just before I call the witness, a small housekeeping matter. The Trial Chamber is seized of the motion for permission to replace transcript references for Exhibits P84 and P85. Shall we perhaps move into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are you going to keep the curtain down. You may proceed, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MP-238, prior to today were you given an opportunity to review your statement of May and June 2008 bearing the 65 ter number 9393?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were to be asked the same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In essence I'm certain that they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter number 9393 at paragraphs 1 through 9, 12, 26, and 29 through 30 into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 9393 at those paragraphs is admitted into evidence under seal. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P460 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MP-238, prior to today were you also given an opportunity to review your transcript from the Dragomir Milosevic case? And for the record the transcript of 19 February 2007 bears the 65 ter number 9394, and the transcript of 20 February 2007 bears the 65 ter number 9395. Sir, had you had an opportunity to review that transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have been given the opportunity to read the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that read back you had indicated that a few items needed to be clarified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically, with regards to the transcript of 19 February 2007, bearing 65 ter number 9394, you indicated that on page 2476 at line 5, the term "few gas aerial bomb" is incorrect, that this was actually, fugasno, f-u-g-a-s-n-o, aerial bomb, as in Fugasno-razorne, r-a-z-o-r-n-e; second word, Avio, a-v-i-o, hyphen, bombe, b-o-m-b-e. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. That was the essence of my comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From page 2459 at lines 17 through 20, the quote from the transcript indicates: "The shell hit the window of the gym, and luckily, if it had been activated 10 centimetres to the other side, it would have come directly through the window." You've indicated that "luckily" is believed to be a translation error and incorrect, unfortunately or another term was to be intended; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct that was my comment. Because it would have been fortunate had the bomb hit a few centimetres higher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From page 2473 at lines 9 and 10, "These were meant to be used for plane travel and now they were used for bombs," is the quote. The term "plane travel" you've indicated was misinterpreted. "These were meant to be dropped out of planes," is the intended language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, these were aerial bombs, and they were meant to be fired or dropped off an aeroplane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After those clarifications had been made, if you were asked those same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter numbers 9394 and 9395 into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As one exhibit? Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to the correction made from lines 10 through -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, from lines 10 through line 15, the answer given by the witness indicating that there's a translation error, I have no difficulty with. However, since we do have, I believe, in its original in audio the answer given by the witness at the time, I would ask that what is done in that regard is that the audio is re-examined so that we can make a determination precisely what was said by the witness. Because here there is a speculative answer of which I have no difficulty in terms of what the gentleman has said just now, but to the extent that we do have an actual answer in a previous proceeding in a transcript that can be captured, I suggest the appropriate thing to do at the time would be to have a re-examination of the audio, and other than that, I have no objection whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What actually is speculative about the witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Unfortunately, now I've gone up on the page. If you give me a second, I'll have to capture the language. "You've indicated that 'luckily' is believed to be a translation error and incorrect. Unfortunately or another term was to be intended; is that correct?" And the speculative part is "unfortunately or another term was intended -- was to be intended." Clearly the answer given by the gentleman at the time is either, A, a translation error; or, B, something else. In the simplest way of making a determination, first of all, of whether or not there has been a translation error is to re-examine the audio of that particular question and answer given. And that's all I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I guess the parties can do that. The witness here has told us that that is how he was misinterpreted, and he wanted to correct this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The difficulty is I think that what you are then left with is an ambiguity in the transcript if it's going to help the Chamber. If the Chamber is satisfied, so be it. But the answer given is -- the answer would now be that the shell hit the window of the gym and unfortunately, or another term that I intended to give, if it had been activated to the other side, it would have come directly through the window. I don't know if that helps the Chamber particularly, but if the Chamber is satisfied with the answer, then I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MP-238, is there any other term that you intended other than "unfortunately," and if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's as follows: The place where the shell impacted, had it been 10 centimetres higher, this shell would have hit another room and the accident would have been avoided, so it's simple really to understand. It had landed at the very edge of the window causing many people to be killed. Had it gone a little higher, it would have hit another room and then no one would have been killed. So it would have been fortunate had this shell gone a little bit higher, and it's unfortunate that it actually hit the edge of the window causing these many deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I leave it to the parties if they want to check the audio of the previous transcripts. They can do so, and they can report back to the Trial Chamber. Madam Carter, do you want these as two separate exhibits, or do you want them as one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As they were given two separate 65 ter numbers, Your Honour, it believe it would be easier to have two separate exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Registrar, will you please assign exhibit numbers to those two 65 ter numbers and give them --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 9394 will be Exhibit P461 under seal; and 65 ter number 9395 will be Exhibit P462 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness MP-238, while you were reviewing your transcript, you also had the opportunity to review the exhibits that had been tendered through that transcript; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. While you were having your transcript read back to you, did you have the opportunity to review exhibits that had been tendered through you in that transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, I did this simultaneously, so I studied the transcript and also compared the items that were being under discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now seeking to adopt those exhibits into your transcript as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, what do you mean "as well"? What do you mean by "adopt"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you believe that those documents are true and accurate documents and you wish to have them a part of your transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the witness wishes to have a part of his transcript or not is irrelevant. I think the question as posed is absolutely improper and does not achieve forensic purpose that the Prosecution wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure -- Madam Carter, I would suggest that you ask the questions the way you want to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, again, I would ask, the documents that you reviewed during your transcript and the statements that you made about them within the transcript, would you ask to adopt those documents as part of your complete record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution seeks to tender 65 ter number 7194, which was P250 in the previous transcript admitted at transcript 2448, which purports to be a photograph of an impact site marked by the witness in case number IT-98-291. Additionally, 65 ter number 7195 which is previously admitted as Exhibit P251 at transcript page 2451, a photo of impact site marked by witness in case number IT-98-291. 65 ter number 8591 previous Exhibit number P252, admitted at transcript page 2452, a criminal investigation file. 65 ter number 8592, prior Exhibit number P253 at transcript T-2455 which is an extract from the criminal investigation file P253 in case number IT-98-291. 65 ter number 7197, previous Exhibit number P254, admitted at transcript T-2457, a diagram and estimates of missile bomb impact on the ground marked by witness in case number IT-98-291. And finally, 65 ter number 7200, previous Exhibit number P256, admitted at transcript page T-2463, a report on Simon Bolivar elementary school incident of 18 June 1995. We seek to tender all of these under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Carter. Madam Registrar, will you please assign Exhibit numbers to all those 65 ter numbers under seal starting with 7194.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 7149 will be Exhibit P463 under seal. 65 ter 7195 will be Exhibit P464 under seal. 65 ter 8591 will be Exhibit P465 under seal. 65 ter 8592 will be Exhibit P466 under seal. 65 ter 7197 will be Exhibit P467 under seal. And 65 ter 7200 will be Exhibit P468 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, for clarity of the record, when reviewing this witness's transcripts from the prior case, there are two Exhibits that were exhibited through him during the Dragomir Milosevic case which have been previously tendered in this one, ergo the Dragomir Milosevic. Exhibit P259 addressed at his transcript 2471 is actually P120 in the present case, and Exhibit P260 admitted at previous transcript 2476 is now P452 in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand the transcript. You may have said something different, Madam Carter, at line 25 of page 11, it says, "previously tendered in this one, ergo if there Dragomir ..." I'm not quite sure what is that. Can you correct that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, my intention was that Dragomir Milosevic Exhibit 259 addressed at his transcript 2471 is actually P120 in the present case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But the line above that, Madam Carter, if it says there are two exhibits that were exhibited through him during the Dragomir Milosevic case, "which have been previously tendered in this one ergo if they," that's just that part that I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, frankly, I'm not certain what I said at that moment. It may be an ergo, as in e-r-g-o, but even that doesn't make very good sense to me. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very. Okay. So what did you want to say about all these exhibits now, now that we don't know what "one ergo" means.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Specific, Your Honour, Exhibit 259 in the Dragomir Milosevic case is Exhibit P120 in the present case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And Exhibit P260 in the Dragomir Milosevic case is now P452 in the present case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you don't want us to do anything, you are telling us those are already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, just for ease of the record, if you are going back and reviewing the transcript from the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, MP-238, I just would like to clarify one aspects of your previous testimony from pages 2435 to 2451 from February 19th of 2007, and that is now Exhibit number P461.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to pull up the Exhibit 464 in the present case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the previous trial there were approximately 20 pages dedicated to determining the angle of the Markale 2 impact. The number 170 was being addressed; and the numbers 220 were being addressed. And you created this diagram at the behest of the Prosecution. If you could, could you please explain what the 170 that we see on this document is intended to signify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to correct you. It is not the angle of incidents. This is the azimuth, being the direction of the shell, so what you see here is 175 degrees of the azimuth which is the direction from which the shell came and then impacted on the marked spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about the possibility of the azimuth being 220, and in that explanation, this graph was drawn. Can you please explain to the Court what is it that you see from the crime scene that takes away the possibility that 220 degree azimuth is appropriate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shell leaves the most evident trace and gives the most information about the angle of incidence when it impacts a solid surface which is concrete or asphalt. On the basis of the crater on the solid surface which is actually marked by this red ellipsoid form, we determine the angle to be 170 which is a vertical in respect of that direction defined as such. So when the shell falls on a solid surface, the trace of the explosion provides us with such information that we can determine with a high degree of reliability the direction of the arrival of the shell. So today we can still ascertain those directions on the basis of such information even though so many years have elapsed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And would the witness please slow down a bit for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are being asked to slow down, sir, so that the interpret can keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your answer you use several terms of art that I would like to have clarified. When you speak of the "trace of the explosion," what specifically are you talking about and what are we seeing on this picture that is "trace"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we can distinguish the place where the fuse actually touched upon the surface and by its initial explosion caused a further explosion. We can recognise the relatively circular portion which is asymmetrical because of the angle of incidents of the shell of the greatest damage on the surface which is a trace left by any anti-infantry shell which is constructed so that most of the shrapnel, the maximum of its lethal effect is actually achieved at that height. So the shell is constructed thus that the strongest effect, lethal effect is achieved a relatively lull in respect of the surface of the ground because it is anti-personnel, anti-infantry shell which intended to kill personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do apologise for interrupting, but my client cannot hear at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, we have a problem. Can somebody help. Can you just say something, Mr. Witness, let's check whether Mr. Perisic can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, voice check. Testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that okay? Thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you are speaking about the fuse actually touching the surface in regards to the initial explosion. What specifically are we seeing on this photograph that speaks to the fuse touching the surface?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The place where the fuse hit is this red spot in the middle, in the centre on the ground, which is enhanced, and the ring surrounding that particular spot actually indicates the direction from which the shell came. Because as a rule, the angle of incidence of a shell is, as a rule, under 90 degrees. The explosion therefore, does not leave a completely concentric circle which would correspond to a 90-degree impact or descent which is impossible. So as a rule, the density of the shrapnel and the depth in the ground is always a picture which reflects or which shows where it is deepest and strongest from where the shell came. This just as if you placed an open umbrella on the ground, it would lean towards one side and where it actually touches the soil, that is the spot of the deepest trace and the deepest impact, or the strongest impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this photograph, what items allow us to understand that this azimuth did come in at 170 degrees as opposed to the 220 degrees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the identification of the most dense and most deep traces of the impact effect of shrapnel which is marked on this figure by this deformed ellipsoid, or this eyebrow shape to be more precise, looking from the spot where the fuse hit which is this red spot, to what is the ellipsoid form, we are actually looking in the direction from which the shell came. When a compass, in this case military compasses, which has a mirror and a thin cord to adjust the direction with, and enhanced preciseness in the mirror, it is possible to read directly on the compasses the azimuth which is 170 degrees. It is a very simple technique, in fact, but it is a very precise technique at the same time which scouts, boy scouts are also familiar with. This is one of the very first things they learn for orientation purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, again going back to the eyebrow shape that you are referring to, obviously the 220 degree azimuth is also intersecting that same eyebrow. Can you be specific why is the position of the eyebrow where it currently not indicative of a 220 degree azimuth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very simply, because the assumed azimuth of 220 degrees intersects this, let us call it, eyebrow, not in the middle, but around one-third of it. The intersection of that deformity on the ground has -- on the ground has to be along its centre, along the axis of symmetry. It has to cut along its middle from the place where the fuse was activated towards the middle, towards the centre, the half of that deformity. And that is how we get the direction and can read the 170 degrees. The direction of 220 degrees also, I repeat, intersects this geometrical figure, but not in half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That certainly make it is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That's the completion of the direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Carter. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss with you your investigation of the incident on June 18th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you just remind me, is it this incident or some other incident? Can you be a bit more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely. It's the incident involving the school, and the -- what I believe was a water collection area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. Now I know what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In your investigation of that incident, when you were investigating the incident, the projectile that you were investigating, the tail-fin was in a position different than the explosion, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you be please more specific. What do you mean when you say the "tail-fin was in a different position"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Your investigation with regard to that particular incident indicated that the tail-fin had continued on a point of trajectory after the explosion had occurred. I think that's a fair way of saying it; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now you have formulated it well, and this is exactly what happened. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for your confidence in my formulation of the question. When -- when that occurred in this particular incident, and as a general matter, the tail-fin, the presence of the tail-fin then is not particularly helpful in making a determination of the direction of travel, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, shall I suggest that once you have asked your question, you switch off your mike because we are on voice distortion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, it is a fact that the tail-fin continued and went into the other room because it was drawn in by the huge vacuum created by the explosion in its centre. And this is what the other traces also show, that the explosion actually happened, took place at a lower sill of the window. And this only actually rounds off the picture of an explosion which happened at that particular section of the window, the lower section of the window's edge because the tail-fin continued into the other room. But as a rule, the position of the tail-fin does not provide much information about the descent, about the fall of a shell on solid ground. Sometimes it actually bounces off, I mean the tail-fin, just bounces off to one side, and sometimes it is riveted into solid ground. And if the ground is soft, then it actually is lodged in quite deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thank you for your answer, but I believe you misapprehended my question, which is whether or not the tail-fin was of assistance in determining the direction from which the projectile came, and in this situation it was not. That your investigation, examination of the tail-fin itself, did not help you in determining the direction from which the projectile came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right, in the sense that it is not possible to use the tail-fin position to determine the direction. The tail-fin provides information about the calibre, the year of manufacture. Very often it does, and very often also about the type of the shell used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this particular incident, there was media information concerning where this particular shell came from, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. That evening, the evening of that tragic event, I heard on the television that the shell had come from Lukavica which is approximately from the east which is absolutely impossible because a mortar shell does not have such a trajectory, nor does any shell has -- make such a yaw in its trajectory, so that I checked actually checked to re-establish the facts and to be satisfied myself of the traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to -- with regard to that particular issue which is the report from the media, can you tell us, if you know, where the media received their information that would make such a report drawing the conclusion that the shell came from a direction quite distinct from that which you believed it came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where the media got their information from, but at any rate, that information was completely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you hold the position that you have held previously in your testimony that -- once again with regard to this particular issue, that concerning the media, they often portray distorted pictures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We witnesses during the war, prior the war, after the war, and today, that just as they do carry the absolute truth, they very often, the media that is, distorted the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to this particular incident, it is your position that the media's reporting portrayed a distorted, as you put it, fact; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I absolutely adhere to my earlier statement, and now I confirm that the media carried a wrong piece of information. Why that information was created and how it came to be published as such, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have 1D00-4563 brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that after your investigation, investigation was done by a team from the United Nations military observer unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. They were also interested in that case, and they arrived at the scene and made some measurements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to the rules of this court, am I to assume that Defence counsel intends to bring Mr. Thomas Hansen as a witness in this case, otherwise it would be an inappropriate use of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am not positive whether or not we intend on bringing Mr. Hansen or not, and I do not believe it is an inappropriate use of his statement because to my knowledge, Mr. Hansen has not testified previously. If I'm mistaken on that regard, then what I would like to do is, first of all, have clarification on that, and then I'll move from that to my next position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I understand what you are saying, Mr. Guy-Smith. I do understand that you are saying you are not positive whether or not you intend calling Mr. Hansen. And that you do not believe that it is inappropriate to use his statement. From then on, I don't understand the rest of that sentence and the rest of your remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if I might, this should probably be done outside the presence of the witness, but I believe that if Ms. Carter is referring to the guide-lines, she's incorrect. Specifically if that is the world in which we are in, let's, first of all, make that as a determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, any specific rule you want to refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, I refer to Rule 12: "The parties may confront a witness in court with a statement of another witness or transcript of prior testimony from another case before this Tribunal only when that person will come to testify in the present case."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith. You said Rule 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a second, Mr. Guy-Smith. My Rule 12 talks of determinations of courts of any state. And it says: "Subject to Article 10, paragraph 2 of the statute, determinations of Courts of any state" --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: She's referring to the guide-lines, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not a rule. Okay. Thank you, Madam Carter. Now, do you have any response to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is something -- first of all, this was an issue that was raised the time that the guide-lines were being promulgated and something that the Defence objected to at that time because of our concerns of the double standard and the -- that it would create as well as -- the double standards that would create a number of different respects, not only that it would force the Defence to put on affirmative evidence in a situation where, simply put, cross-examination would become the vehicle whereby we could test the Prosecution evidence. And that in this situation, the rule as constituted caused a problem. So we have previously objected to it. With regard to whether or not we intend on calling this particular witness, I cannot say that we will at this point in time call this particular witness. What I would suggest that we do, because there are now two issues that are raised, is, one, that I be allowed to examine the witness with regard to Thomas Hansen's statement; that, two, the Chamber can make a determination as to whether or not it wishes to consider it or not at a later point in time; and, three, the issue that had been previously presented during the time that we were going through the discussion of the guide-lines has now crystallized, and we now are in a position to further brief it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith, I hear that you previously objected to this thing, but, however, at this stage it is part of the guide-lines, and the guide-line is quite clear that unless you are going to call the witness to testify later, you may not use his statement to confront this witness. And I think you have to make a determination whether or not you are going to call this witness, and if you are not -- if you say you are not sure, I'm afraid according to that guide-line you may not use this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, once again, I respectfully disagree. And I disagree for the following reason, which is that paragraph 13 indicates that where a witness is confronted in Court with a statement or transcript of another witness who is scheduled to come and testify in the present case, and in our situation we don't have somebody who is scheduled to testify in the present case because the Defence case certainly has not yet come to the fore, the Prosecution has not yet completed their case. There's question as to whether or not the Prosecution will even meet their burden. So although it would put us in a slightly different situation, in the event that Mr. Hansen was scheduled to testify as a Defence witness and did not testify, then the remedy would be found in paragraph 13. And I'll put in other terms, Your Honour, the rule as constituted causes a series of not only procedural, but actually fair-trial problems under Article 21 for the Defence. And I think you have probably crystallized it in another sense, which is we have no burden at this point to make a determination of what witnesses we are going to be calling. We may call this witness. I do not -- I could say to you at this point in time we are going to call -- we are going to call Mr. Hansen. That would satisfy the initial inquiry. That, however, wouldn't be an accurate statement, and as an officer of the court, not the kind of statement because I, in good faith, can't tell you at this point that it's something that we are going to do. I can tell you in good faith that the statement of Mr. Hansen puts into stark contrast issues that exist with regard to this witness's testimony. I can tell you in good faith, and the Prosecution is well aware of it, that this witness was previously examined about this self-same matter, that the Prosecution had previously through cherry-picking made a determination not to call Thomas Hansen as a witness, and that it puts us in an untenable position because we are now being forced to make a determination of whether or not we are going to be calling witnesses prior to the time that you have even made a determination whether the Prosecution has proved their case beyond a reasonable doubt to your satisfaction at a half time submission. If you want me to say for purposes of a record something that I can't accurately say, I can say, Yes, we intend on calling -- we intend on calling Mr. Hansen in the event that this Chamber makes a determination at the half time submission that the Prosecution has met their burden. I can say that. And then if I don't call him at a later point in time, you would rightfully criticize me, and you would ask me whether or not at the time that I made this statement I was being honest with you. And I'm not in the habit of not being honest with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I think you should look at paragraph 12 and 13, those two paragraphs are governing two different situations. In the one situation in paragraph 12, the situation where the witness is not going to be called. If you can only do so, you can only confront the witness here with a statement of a witness that you intend to call. Okay. Paragraph 13 deals with a situation where, in fact, you have determined that you are going to call the witness and you have scheduled him, but for one or other reason, the witness does not turn up. At that stage it's -- paragraph 13 deals with a situation that arises which had not been planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if that situation arises at that stage, then that is the remedy. To suggest now at this stage that because you have not made a determination whether or not to call Hansen, therefore we must then take resort in paragraph 13 is -- is this as you say, you want to be honest with the Court and tell it exactly where you stand? I'm not forcing you to say you are going to call this person or not call him, but this situation envisaged in paragraph 13 is a situation where something happened which had not been planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand what you've said, Your Honour, and I think that paragraph 13 is instructive of what to do where -- where there is a prior testimony or a prior statement from a witness which because the witness has not been called to testify, the Chamber has a mechanism whereby to deal with that particular evidence. But I'm dealing with a more fundamental issue, quite frankly, which is this, Which is why I said that we had objected to it initially and why the issue exists now: As this is presently drafted, if Ms. Carter's position is the position that this Chamber is going to call -- going to adopt with regard to our ability to cross-examine, to use the crucible of cross-examination as a basis upon which this Chamber makes a determination about whether the Prosecution has met its burden of proof, then our hands are effectively tied in a number of areas. Because if the Prosecution has gone out and taken a statement and then by virtue of the fact the statement is beneficial to the Defence and detrimental to the Prosecution, they choose not to present that evidence to the Chamber in the fullness of the presentation that they are supposed to make seeking justice, then we are left in a position where you are foreclosed from having the information by virtue of the fact that we are supposed to tell you who we intend to call. And we have no burden at this point to call anyone whatsoever. We have not reached that point in these proceedings. The burden, if at all, is the burden upon the Prosecution in their case in chief to present the evidence. It is not for us at this point in time to labour under the assumption that we are going to have to call witnesses. Otherwise -- otherwise the burden of proof has absolutely no meaning whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The burden of proof has every meaning, sir. Even if you relied on paragraph 13, if at the stage of 98 bis proceedings you decide not to call any witness and we have to assess the testimony that has been given by the Prosecution witnesses, at that stage you will have not called Hansen, and whatever you may have used from Hansen's statement to confront this witness would be valueless.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But you see, Your Honour, therein truly lies the rub. I mean, and I'm asking you for a moment to reflect upon the situation that we are in. Hansen's statement directly has relevant evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me finish, please. It was obtained by the Prosecution with regard to this incident. It's evidence that they don't care for, and that's been established in a prior proceeding when they chose to drop him from the witness list. This is the -- this is the most -- this is the most clear example of cherry-picking that you can possibly have in a case where now evidence that they know could objectively, objectively be considered by the Chamber independent about whether he is called, independent of that issue, is now being foreclosed because of the rule that they suggest exists now at a point in time when I have no burden whatsoever to call a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I want to believe that you understood what I'm saying. I'm saying, yes, I agree with you. You have no burden to call a witness, and therefore at the close of the Prosecution case, it will be as if you have not even called -- you don't expect this Court when you have not -- when you are burdened to call a witness that has not arisen to then consider the testimony of a person that has not been called simply because it was used to confront this witness. And I'm saying to you, if you will not interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm saying to you at that stage, if you decide to rest the Defence case without calling a witness, we couldn't -- the Chamber cannot use Mr. Hansen's statement in evaluating this witness's testimony because at that stage Mr. Hansen is not a witness. And the question of cherry-picking by the Prosecution, I will not comment on. I do not control the Prosecution. The Prosecution is independent. They choose who they want to call as a witness, and they conduct their case the way they want to conduct it. But I just want to say to you, you may go along paragraph 13. Do know, however, that if Hansen is not called as paragraph 13 does say, the Chamber will not take into regard what effect he had --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand the position. I believe there is an underlying legal principle that's being lost as a result of the guide-lines as they've been promulgated, first of all, with all due respect. Second of all, I think that we will find that another anomaly will occur as we go on when we enter into the mysterious world of 92 quater, but I reserve my remarks about 92 quater problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, can we deal with the point at issue and forget 92 quater.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think I would like to do the following, which is I would like to examine this gentleman with regard to Mr. Hansen's statement at this time. I also would like to and will be filing a motion with regard to the Chamber's reconsideration of paragraph 12 as it's constituted. In the event that the Chamber makes a determination that paragraph 12 will remain the same, I will be seeking -- and I'm telling you now because I think this is a point of some importance. I will be seeking review of that because I think the issue that is presented here is an issue which is fundamental to the entirety of these proceedings. That is one possibility and one mechanism to proceed forward. Another way to proceed forward, is I would at this time move for admission and making an offer of proof as to what the questions would be that I would ask this gentleman and move for admission three separate exhibits which then would perfect the record so that the Chamber would be in a position to see precisely why it is necessary not only, one, to allow for this kind of examination to occur in the view of the Defence, but be in a position to have all of the information. So I'm in the Chamber's hands as to how to proceed. But I'm not going to say to you at this point in time that I intend to call somebody who I cannot in good faith say that I am or am not intending to call. I just won't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the Chamber has made clear what is likely to happen depending on what developments take place in the future. And if you are relying on paragraph 13, you may go ahead and use the statement, but I think the Chamber has made it clear what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm actually going beyond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am sorry, I will not deal with issues that are not before me now. I know that you have mentioned that you have three separate exhibits that you intend to tender, we don't really want that. I am really on this statement now. You can use it, and we will watch as the trial goes on whether this man gets called or not, doesn't get called. If you want to deal with exhibits later, you can deal exhibits later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to allow the conversation to continue before I interject on this as well. There are still other provisions in paragraph 12 that we must be cognizant of, specifically that we can't un-ring the bell, but it says: "The presenting party must identify to the Trial Chamber and the other party the name of the statement, make or prior of the witness, the date of the statement or transcript, and page references of the portions statement of the transcript which will be read out in Court or referred to. However, this information shall not be disclosed to the witness in court. The second it was brought up on the screen, we were already in violation of the guide-lines. While we certainly understand he can cross-examine this witness on anything within his knowledge if he has a reasonable basis for asking the question, however, to do it in this specific manner is a clear violation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you will make sure, therefore, to the extent that you can still comply with 12, paragraph 12, make sure you do comply with paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would at this point then ask that the witness be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be excused. Shall we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told you asked that the witness not be brought in yet, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. Very briefly, I'm going to be questioning -- because of the concerns raised by Ms. Carter and because I want to try to keep whatever issues ultimately presented as pure as possible with regard to the variety of matters, I have informed Ms. Carter and I will inform the Chamber that I intend on cross-examining the witness concerning a statement made by Thomas last name is Hansen, H-a-n-s-e-n. The statement was taken on the 8th and 9th of September 1995 by interviewers Jan van Hecke, that's H-e-c-k-e and Todd Cleaver. I'm going to be asking him questions specifically in relation to page 2 which is identified as ERN number 0064-6492, the last full paragraph. And page 3, which would be of course the next ERN number in order. With regard to paragraphs 2 -- I believe -- I don't know if I have mentioned 2 to you, before, Ms. Carter. 2, 3, 4, and 8, and I'm counting them off just because these are not numbered paragraphs. This was a statement that was taken, as I understand it, by the Office of the Prosecutor and was forwarded to us pursuant to Rule 68. And with that being said, we can then call in the witness. But to the extent that Ms. Carter indicated there were some concerns about guide-line paragraph 12, I want to make sure that we don't run into any further difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any comments to make, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may call the witness. May we move into private session for the purposes of the witness's entry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to read something to you and ask you some questions about it, okay. I'm now referring the Court and counsel to the matter that we discussed in the absence of the witness beforehand, and I'm referring the Court and counsel to page 2: "I think we finally arrived on the scene about" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have that page 2 now that it is not displayed on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is there -- I ask the usher, is there a way of displaying the page to the Chamber and to not have it displayed on the screen for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that possible? Is that possible, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it's being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, to facilitate, I actually have hard copies of the document that at issue in triplicate for the Court. I just notifying Mr. Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That on the top right corner, I did write the previously exhibit number and the place that it was admitted in the transcript, but that's the only writing that was on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine, not a problem. I thank you for your assistance in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm referring to page 2, the bottom paragraph which starts with the words "I think ..." "I think we finally arrived on the scene about 1 to 1 and a half hour after impact. At the time we arrived, the Bosnian police had already carried out their investigation, and the investigation team had left." Before I go any further, when you were engaged in your investigation, did you engage in your investigation with any other team? Were there any other people there investigating at the time that you were investigating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The team that conducted the investigation was a mixed team. The local Sarajevo police, the so-called CSB had a team of, I think, some seven members, two of whom were from a higher level from the ministry of police. One of them being myself, and the other, a member from the KDZ. So we conducted an investigation because it was our responsibility. It was our obligation to do after our flag was recognised in New York. So as a state, we were the ones who had the right and obligation to conduct this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At the time that you were conducting the investigation with the mixed team that you discussed, were there, to your knowledge, any international teams conducting an investigation of the same incident that you were conducting the investigation of on June 18th at the school, at that time while you were doing your investigation on site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard to say. I can't claim that I recall that. It is possible that toward the end of the investigation, there were some other people there taking part in it, but I cannot be more specific. I do know that after our investigation there were some, let's call them foreigners who also conducted an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to continue: "Anyway, we were accompanied by a Bosnian official when we went to the scene. The only thing we could see at the scene was an impact on the west side of a wall 4 metres above ground level and some blood and brains and human parts." I'll stop there. When you were engaged in your investigation, did you see an impact point approximately 4 metres above ground level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the key detail in conducting an investigation, or this particular investigation. As such, it was prominent in the next following days. Of course, based on this, we concluded the direction from which the shell came and the azimuth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I take it would it be fair to say that with regard to the blood and other human remains that were found, you also, during the time that you were investigating the matter, saw that too, and unfortunately so, but you saw that too; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course because the bodies were dismembered, the killed people had been massacred and dismembered taken away before we came so that when we arrived we saw huge quantity of blood and parts of brains because the explosion came from above the people's heads, and this is what we saw when we arrived at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I continue: "By seeing the impact, in my opinion the shell came from the west, eventually from the north-west. The tail-fin was already removed by the Bosnian police and the victims were brought to Dobrinja hospital." Now, my question to you is, were you involved in removing the tail-fin, and there's nothing wrong with that obviously, from the site during your investigation? Is that something that you were involved in doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The investigating team always in events such as these collects the material traces of the origin of the fact. The tail-fin is the crown exhibit, the crown piece of evidence about the type of the incident, and the traces at the spot of the explosion are actually proof about the direction, the azimuth of the arrival of the shell. I personally did not remove the tail-fin. It is a routinely collected with other parts, with other segments, and it is taken to the KDZ centre for further analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, were the victims brought to the Dobrinja hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the victims were taken to the Dobrinja mortuary, to the morgue, it was by the Dobrinja hospital, and it was used very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I continue: "So we could not do a proper investigation. By the way the shell hit the wall it was obvious that the shell was fired from a roughly west position." With regard to that statement, does that statement comport with your investigation? And by that I mean that the shell was fired from a roughly west position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, however, the claim that the shell came from either the west or the north-west is much more imprecise, and in our finding we ascertain that it had come from the north-west. And these two claims are not on a collision course. But this other assertion is more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. According to your determination, which site did it come from? I heard something slightly different on the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our finding, the shell had come from the direction which is shown by the azimuth which is the north-west direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm now going to page 3 for the Chamber's and counsel's information, starting on the second paragraph: "In the hospital, a Bosnian official showed me a tail-fin that he said they found at the scene. It was definitely a tail-fin of 120 millimetre shell." Were you involved in showing anyone at the hospital a tail-fin concerning the incident on June 18th? And by that I mean, were you personally involved, yes or no, in showing any international -- let me make the question a little more precise, any international, a tail-fin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tail-fin, not me. No, I was not at the hospital. I had no occasion, nor did I -- was I in possession of that tail-fin, nor did I show it to internationals. Probably it was someone from this team who took the foreigners to the hospital, and as they had taken the tail-fin as a material piece of evidence for further analysis, they probably could have shown it to them. Why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. "Of course it was impossible for me to know ..." I continue with the statement. "Of course it was impossible for me to know if this was a tail-fin of this incident, but there was no reason to lie about this. Because we could not carry on investigation, we could not confirm the findings of the Bosnian police." My question at this point is, did you ever have a joint meeting -- once again, I'm talking about you personally. Did you ever have a joint meeting or a joint discussion with the international investigation team concerning this particular incident? Once again, it's always the incident on June 18th, the school incident. Did you do that personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall having participated in any such joint meeting myself. However, the international forces wanted to be seen as our supervisors, like it was that we sometimes knew things, sometimes did not, and they always knew what was the case. I think it was just the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, when you say you think it was just the opposite, I take it -- I'm not sure what you mean by that. What was just the opposite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm saying that it is the opposite in the material since. That is, that the international forces should be our supervisors, because in such instances, in such cases we have a far vaster experience, we had, than the international forces. Just as war surgeons had by far a greater war experience as surgeons than the -- their counterparts in London. They had a three-year experience by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand what you are saying now. What you are saying is that the international forces took the position that they always knew what was the case. And as a matter of fact, you think -- it's your opinion that by virtue of your experience on the ground that that wasn't accurate at all, that they were not the people who knew what was going on all the time but rather you people who had been experiencing the situation and had been involved in a great number of investigations were the individuals who actually knew what was happening? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your question is not exactly precise, but a large number of cases confirm exactly what you have said and what I'm stating.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll continue with what the statement says: "The only thing we could determine was that the general direction of the firing had to be west to north-west. When you see the confrontation line west to north-west from the point of impact, it is almost impossible to determine whether the shell was fired by a BiH or a BSA mortar. With a possible ranges for a 120 millimetre shell, it could have been fired from either side." Now, my first question is this: With regard to the issue of possible ranges of a 120 millimetre shell, could you tell us what the possible ranges are of such a shell, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gentlemen's claim that the shell could have been fired from the west from our positions is a claim --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, I hate to interrupt you. I ask you a very specific question, and then I will ask you other questions. My first question is this: With regard to the issue of possible ranges of a 120 millimetre shell, could you possibly tell us what the ranges are of such a shell, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of kilometres. However, the range figures have faded from my memory. But it is a big range of that shell, it is impossible to fire from a close range which would correspond to its having been fired from our positions which is a couple of metres, a couple of hundred metres. That would be as if a plane took off from this courtroom here as its runway, which is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that the confrontation line with -- in relationship to the school was a couple of hundred metres away? Is that what you are telling us here? And by a couple of hundred metres, I take it you mean 200 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the place where the shell fell to the west towards Nedzarici, it is indeed a couple of hundred metres, but not -- 200 metres, a bit more than that. But that can be established from looking at a map. We can establish the exact number of metres. In looking in hindsight from today, the line of separation towards the west and its distance from the place where the shell impacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you were doing your investigation on the 18th, and did you at that time take into account the confrontation line and the location of your forces in relationship to the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not an essential factor in the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it your answer would be, no, you did not do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We used a map which this [indiscernible] Tribunal is familiar with. I've seen it in my previous giving of testimony, and I drew in the precise line of the azimuth and the firing position from the location in Nedzarici. And that map shows exactly the line of separation, the positions of the other party, and that is quite clear on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were involved in investigations in 1995, were you aware of the fact that your army had captured mortar shells from the enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain that I understand this question, but in every occasion we capture shells in order to defend ourselves and we manufacture our own whenever we were in a position to do so. So the assumption does not stand that we were bare-handed and would take something which belongs to another. Of course, we did take all ordinals that we could lay our hands on in the course of the exchange of fire, and we used them for our Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly meant no insult there in terms of your capabilities or the amount that you had military assets. So let me ask you this question: During this period of time, would it be fair to say that your army was in possession of mortars and included in that were mortars that were 120 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course we were in possession of them, and we produced, manufactured most of the shells for these mortar in several towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina because we had very competent personnel in our industry in Bosnia who were capable of manufacturing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina were you manufacturing these mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance in Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there were several other organised manufacturing facilities, but I do not know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "several," without knowing the details, could you tell us how many, and by that I mean the word several could mean two, it could mean ten, and if you could give us a number of other manufacturing facilities that you were aware of during this period of time, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I was a member of a special police detachment for investigations of the time that we are discussing. All the details associated with military tactics, strategy, and logistics is something I was not privy to and was not familiar with, nor were they informed about that. As a recognised, internationally recognised country, we could and were able to manufacture weapons for our own defence because the embargo actually did not apply to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say the embargo did not apply to you, could you tell the Chamber which embargo you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the arms embargo, but you did not hear me properly. It was mistranslated. What I said was, that the embargo for the import of arms applied to only Bosnia-Herzegovina, everybody else had free access to the arms trade, and it was indeed a very vigorous trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were there issues concerning a request by your government at the time to lift that embargo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were countless requests to that effect by our minister of the -- of foreign affairs at that time, who I think was Haris Silajdzic and all international meetings. And in such context we requested for that embargo to be lift because it was detrimental to only the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And with leave of the Court, based on this examination of this document, it brings up two other documents that were submitted to the Prosecution by the Defence as potential exhibits that I would like to address in the redirect examination. It's coming strictly from what was brought out in the cross-examination. These are not on our original 92 ter package, but we do believe that the door has now been opened to use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying that the Defence did refer to those documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When the Defence was making their submissions earlier and they indicated that there were multiple documents at issue along with the statement that we've just been referring to, these are the documents that I am now referring to that I would like to be able to use them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but my question is, did the Defence use them?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The Defence did not use them yet, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why would you then want to use them, Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Because the Defence has now brought into question the line of fire from that shell, and these documents provided by the Defence would allow us to address that more fully and more completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any comments, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Submitted. No comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The document that was provided to us by the Defence had Defence number D000-4571, but it also maintains a 65 ter number from the Prosecution of 8594. So I'd like to have it brought up under 8594, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that a document that you are now going to expose to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is a UN headquarter daily sitrep as opposed to a statement. Or I can simply ask questions and not have the witness see the document as well. Either is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that is be probably a preferable in this instance, considering the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you were discussing the shell that fell on to the Simon Bolivar school with Defence counsel, and I want to explore that a little further with you. The UN headquarters -- were you aware that the UN headquarters was monitoring all of the activity in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had information that the UN headquarters had a monitoring system of the trajectories of all the artillery weapons about Sarajevo, and they had data about all of the artillery positions about the army of the Bosnian Serbs and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that they knew much more than they would let on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that the UN HQ was actually monitoring every cease-fire violation and firing incident that was taking place in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To the extent that the question goes beyond the cross-examination, I object to it. And it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Simply, Your Honour, to lay the foundation of going directly to what was discussed in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll repeat my question. Would it surprise you that the UN HQ was actually monitoring every cease-fire and firing incident that was taking place in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would not surprise me because I know that they monitored everything, and that suited us. Although there had been some ill-meant interpretations and analyses on the part of the UN troops such as a shooting incident with many people, deaths where the mortar was -- mortar was used with a table used from the -- in the Chinese war, so that the analysis results were quite different. But what you asked me about that, that would not surprise me at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I appreciate that you have quite a familiarity with what occurred in Sarajevo, but if you could please just focus your answers on the question I specifically ask. Sir, on June -- sorry. On June 18th, 1995, would it surprise you that the UNMO had registered 69 cease-fire breaches? Would that seem consistent with your experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well -- I'll let it go.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: On that singular day, would it surprise you that there were 69 cease-fire breaches in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would not surprise me because it was the rule. Every time a cease-fire was proclaimed, there would be a massive shelling following. That was the rule. So that would not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to know if this is consistent with your experience on that day. At date time group 11.46, there was a singular explosion in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It's on page 8 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: That of the day at 11.46, there's a single explosion in Dobrinja, and it was fired by the Bosnian/Serb army, is this consistent with your findings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And, sir, is it also consistent with your experience in Dobrinja that that was the only incident that took place in Dobrinja on 18 June 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was the only one in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter, could you please switch off your microphone when the witness is answering. We are here on voice distortion. And secondly, you are talking of page 8 of a document which we have no access to.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document can go up on e-court at 8594, or I do have hard copies as before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please, ma'am. In fact, I think it would be preferable if it went up here because then it forms part of the record, unless there is any special objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, now that we've discussed the direction of the shell that hit Dobrinja, I would now like to discuss the shell itself. Did your unit have the opportunity to analyse that 120 millimetre shell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, are you referring to the traces which remained there and the tail-fin because this is the shell after the explosion. This is what you have after an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I'm specifically referring to the primary charge and the stabilizer. Did your team have the opportunity to review that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we studied those parts, and more importantly, we also studied the geometry of the trace following the explosion, the trace left on the wall. On the basis of which we concluded what the azimuth was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I thank you, sir, for that. Fortunately in your prior testimony, you were quite verbose in regards to the tracings on the outside, so I want to focus specifically on the shell itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that you take us along with you, Madam Carter, we have the document here, and I'm not sure whether you are discussing the Dobrinja shelling, or are you discussing the shelling of the 18th of June, 1995, which was at a school, Simon Bolivar school. Where are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have moved off of the direction of fire. The indication is -- and within the transcript was that that was registered at 11.40 in Dobrinja. And I what I was attempting to elicit from the witness and for the Court's attention is that there's only one single firing into Dobrinja at all on the 18th. It is consistent with the time that we have indicated, and that the firing position was actually from the Bosnian/Serb army. So I completed that line of questioning. Now I've moved on to the specifics of the investigation and the shell itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But which incident is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It's A7, Your Honour, on 18 June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I ask you this question, Madam Carter, is this incident you are discussing discussed in the witness's statement that has been tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At paragraph 12, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Paragraph 12. Very well. Now, at paragraph 12 the incident that is being discussed there refers to an incident at the Simon Bolivar school. Is that what you are discussing?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I hear you talking of Dobrinja. How does Dobrinja come in? Is this school in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, can you confirm where is the Simon Bolivar school located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simon Bolivar school is in the centre of down-town Dobrinja, that's the new part of the town. It is almost a separate municipality, it's a settlement. And this school was right in the middle of this settlement, so practically it's the same location.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Did that clarify the Court's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I had like to turn your attention to the shell itself, the projectile, and the primary charge and the stabilizer. Did your team --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object. This has been asked and answered and is part of their 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: With all due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, just a second. What has been asked and answered, Mr. Guy-Smith? I haven't heard the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Issues concerning investigations of primary charge and stabilizers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but we don't know what the question is going to be. She is just turning his attention to them, and you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll wait. I'll wait. I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In order to address what was being discussed in the cross-examination, sir, you were asked about the Bosnian's abilities to receive shells from Defence counsel.
